title: IntegrationConfig
description:
AirPipe integration configuration. Defines the structure for API configurations
with interfaces, actions, and global settings.

## Example
```yaml
name: my-api-config           # Required: Name of the configuration
version: 0.1.0                # Optional: Version string
description: My API config    # Optional: Description

global:                       # Optional: Global settings
  variables:                  # Global variables accessible in all interfaces
    api_base_url: https://api.example.com
  secrets:                    # Global secrets (values are encrypted)
    my_secret:
      value: secret_value
  databases:                  # Global database connections
    main_db:
      connection_string: postgres://user:pass@localhost/db

interfaces:                   # Required: Map of interface definitions
  myEndpoint:                 # Interface name (if http used as route, unless route itself is defined)
    method: POST              # HTTP method
    actions:                  # Actions to execute
      - name: ValidateInput
        input: a|body|
```

expose_metrics.description:
Expose a Prometheus `/metrics` endpoint for this config (self-hosted modes only).
When true, interface and action-level metrics are emitted with `{config, interface}` labels.

description.description: Human-readable description of what this configuration does.

docs.description:
Enable or disable auto-generated API documentation for this config's HTTP interfaces.
Defaults to enabled (omit or set true). Set to false to exclude from docs.

interfaces.description:
Map of interface definitions. Keys are interface names (used as routes),
values contain the interface configuration with actions and settings.

global.description:
Global configuration shared across all interfaces including variables,
secrets, databases, templates, and HTTP defaults.

network.description:
Config-wide network access-control policy (IP/geo/ASN/rate-limit). Applies
to every interface as a baseline; each interface inherits and tightens it
via its own `network` block (unless it sets `inherit: false`).

mcp_servers.description:
MCP server identities declared by this config, keyed by server id. The id doubles as the
route segment (`/<org>/<env>/mcp/<id>`), so it is restricted to `[a-z0-9-]{1,64}`.

Declaring a server is independent of contributing tools to it: interfaces in *any* config in
the same org+environment join a server via `mcp.server`, and one entry here marked `default`
adopts every tool that names no server. A config that declares nothing keeps today's
behaviour exactly — its tools join the default server, which falls back to the built-in
identity when no config declares one.

on_error.description:
Run an interface whenever a run of this config fails.

The engine already knows every failure — it decides the status code and records
the run — so this turns that into an alert, a ticket or a dead-letter write
without a second system polling for it.

## Example
```yaml
on_error:
  interface: NotifyOps
  status: [500, 502, 503]
  max_per_minute: 6
```

capture.description:
How much of this interface's runs to record for execution history.

Absent means off, which is also the fleet-wide default: capture is opt-in per interface,
then bounded again by the org's tier, allowance and the node's rate buckets.

defaults.description:
Defaults handed to every action in this interface (see [`ActionDefaults`]). An action
that sets the field itself always wins.

mqtt.description:
MQTT trigger name. When set, this interface is triggered by an MQTT PUBLISH to the
topic `<environment>/<interface_name>/<this value>` (carried over MQTT-over-WebSocket
at `/mqtt`). The published JSON is available to the pipeline as `a|body`.

ws.description:
WebSocket marker. When set (to any value), this interface is reachable over WebSocket at
`/ws/<org>/<environment>/<interface_name>`; each inbound JSON text frame runs the
interface and the result is sent back over the same socket.

subscribe_authorizer.description:
Realtime-channel access control. The name of an interface run to authorize a
socket's `ap_subscribe` to a channel: it runs with `{ "channel": "<name>" }`
as `a|body` and the socket's token as `a|headers::airpipe-jwt|`, and the
subscribe is allowed iff the authorizer returns 2xx (so its `is_valid_jwt` +
claim/channel checks gate it). Unset ⇒ any socket may subscribe to any channel
in its own org. Fail-closed: an anonymous socket (no token) is denied.

public.description:
Public realtime opt-in. When `true`, this WebSocket interface accepts END-USER
connections with NO credential at all — no org API key and no JWT — for non-sensitive
public feeds (live scores, status pages, public presence), matching the "public channel"
model of Ably/Pusher. Channel-level ACL still applies if a `subscribe_authorizer` is set,
and the per-org realtime abuse floors (publish rate, subscriptions, topics, retained)
still bound the interface — so open access cannot be weaponised on shared infra. Default
(unset/false) requires a credential at connect (the safe default).

disable_fastpath.description:
Opt this interface out of the compiled fast path (AP_FASTPATH), forcing every request through
the interpreter. The fast path is byte-identical, so this never changes output — it is an escape
hatch for interfaces where the fast-path attempt's side effects matter on a fallback: a fast-path
attempt that bails (an assert fails) has already fired its side-effecting actions (http requests,
DB writes), and the interpreter then re-runs them, so those side effects fire twice. Set this on
an interface where that double-fire is unacceptable (or, as here, on a test-harness interface
that deliberately fails tests so it would always bail). Default (unset) = fast path allowed.

accepts.description:
What this interface ACCEPTS: the shape of the payload its trigger delivers, and
an example of it.

Transport-neutral on purpose. An interface is not always an HTTP endpoint — it may
be an MQTT subscription, a WebSocket channel, an MCP tool or a cron schedule — and
"request" is only the right word for one of those. A schedule accepts nothing and
simply omits this; an MQTT interface accepts the message published to its topic.

The schema is DERIVED from the interface's `assert` tests when absent (see
[`crate::interface_schema::input_schema`]), so this only needs filling in to
override the derivation or to add an example.

produces.description:
What this interface PRODUCES: the shape of its result, and an example of it.

For an HTTP interface that is the response body; for a schedule it is what the run
yielded; for MQTT/WS it is what the interface publishes. Note this is documentation
of the payload — `response` next to it stays what it always was, the HTTP response
*behaviour* (status codes, headers, fallbacks).

request_example.description:
Example request body shown in generated API documentation.

DEPRECATED: use `request: { example: … }`. Still read so existing configs keep
working; `request.example` wins when both are present.

response_example.description:
Example successful response body shown in generated API documentation.

DEPRECATED: use `response: { example: … }`. Still read so existing configs keep
working; `response.example` wins when both are present.

notes.description: Additional free-form documentation notes shown under the endpoint description.

network.description:
Network access-control policy for this interface (IP/geo/ASN/rate-limit).
Inherits and tightens the config-wide `network` policy unless `inherit: false`.
Evaluated before any actions run; denied requests get the `on_deny` response.

mcp.description:
Expose this interface as an MCP tool (opt-in). When set with `enabled: true`,
the interface is listed by the MCP server (`tools/list`) and callable via
`tools/call`, reusing the interface's existing in-config auth assertions.
Absence = not exposed, so admin/sensitive interfaces simply omit this field.

CaptureSetting.description:
`capture:` on an interface — either a mode, or a mode that switches itself off.

The window form is what keeps the fleet's resting state at "capture off" no matter how many
people click the button. Permanent capture stays a deliberate, tier-gated choice rather than
the easy path.

```yaml
capture: errors                 # plain mode

capture:                        # self-expiring window
  mode: all
  for_minutes: 30
  for_runs: 500                 # whichever comes first
```

CaptureMode.description: How much of a run to record.

oneOf.description: Record nothing. The fleet-wide default.

Record failed runs only.

The mode worth defaulting to when capture is wanted at all: volume then tracks the ERROR
RATE rather than throughput, so a healthy system at a million runs an hour writes almost
nothing, and generating capture load requires generating failures — which the request
rate limiter already governs. Successes are already counted in metrics; a stored row adds
nothing a metric does not.
Record successful runs too. The expensive mode, and the one tiers actually buy.

for_minutes.description: Switch off this many minutes after the window opens.

for_runs.description: Switch off after this many runs.

expect_status.description: Seeds `http.expect_status` on every action of this interface that does not set its own.

StatusExpectation.description: `expect_status:` — either a single matcher or a list of them.

StatusMatcher.description:
One entry in an `expect_status` / `retry.on` list.

Accepts an exact code (`404`), a class (`2xx`, `4xx`, `5xx`), `any`, or — for
`retry.on` only — a transport class (`timeout`, `connect`).

Schedule.description:
AirPipe schedule configuration. Defines when and how an interface should be
executed automatically via the scheduler.

## Example
```yaml
myScheduledEndpoint:        # Interface name
  method: POST
  actions:
    - name: MyAction
      http:
        url: https://api.example.com/trigger

  schedule:                 # Schedule configuration (enables auto-execution)
    cron: "0 9 * * *"       # Required: Cron expression (5 fields: minute-hour-day-month-weekday)
    enabled: true           # Optional: Enable/disable the schedule (default: false)

    # Retry configuration
    max_attempts: 3         # Optional: Max retry attempts on failure (default: 1)
    retry_backoff_seconds: 60    # Optional: Initial backoff in seconds (default: 60)
    retry_backoff_multiplier: 2.0 # Optional: Backoff multiplier for exponential backoff (default: 2.0)
    max_backoff_seconds: 3600    # Optional: Maximum backoff cap in seconds (default: 3600)
```

cron.description: Cron expression in 5-field format (minute hour day month weekday)

max_backoff_seconds.description: Maximum retry backoff cap in seconds

timezone.description: IANA timezone for cron interpretation (e.g. 'America/New_York'); defaults to UTC

replayable.description:
Whether a captured run containing this action may be replayed.

Replay re-runs an action for real, so an action with a side effect the world can see —
charging a card, sending an email, publishing to a topic — must say so. Any action
marked `replayable: false` makes the whole run **inspect-only**, and the run records
which action did it so the answer is "ChargeCard cannot be replayed" rather than a
disabled button with no explanation.

Declared rather than inferred, in the same spirit as `expect_status`: guessing which
actions are safe to repeat is exactly the judgement that should not be automatic. n8n
simply re-runs, and it bites people.

## Example
```yaml
- name: ChargeCard
  replayable: false
```

timeout.description:
Maximum execution time for this action in milliseconds.

## Example
```yaml
timeout: 5000    # 5 seconds
```

input.description:
Where this action's data comes from. Common sources:
- `a|body|` - HTTP request body
- `a|params|` - URL parameters
- `a|action_name::field|` - output from an earlier action

## Example
```yaml
input: a|body|
```

## Example
```yaml
input: a|LoginBody::email|
```

## Closing pipe

`input` accepts the bare form too — `a|body`, with no trailing pipe — because
this field names a source directly rather than interpolating one into a larger
string. It is the only field where that is true.

**Everywhere else the closing pipe is required and its absence is silent.**
`url: https://x/a|body` does not resolve to anything; it sends the literal text
`a|body`, because the scanner that finds references only matches a closed
marker. Nothing warns, and the request goes out wrong.

Write `a|body|` everywhere, including here. The bare form is kept for configs
that already use it and is not offered in new examples.

input_fallbacks.description:
Alternative input sources to try if the primary input is not available.

## Example
```yaml
input_fallbacks:

  - a|params::token|
```

conditional_input.description:
Define conditional input based on runtime conditions.
Uses Simple (list of input strings) or Complex (with tests).

## Example - Simple
```yaml
conditional_input:
  - a|body::premium|      # Try this first
  - a|body::standard|     # Fallback
```

## Example - Complex
```yaml
conditional_input:
  - input: a|body::type|
    tests:
      - is_equal_to: "premium"
```

Name of a lookup configuration to use for pre-fetching data.

## Example

Per-item execution timeout for lookup iterations.
Controls how long each individual item in the lookup array is allowed to run.
Use `timeout` to cap the total loop duration.


Maximum number of lookup items to execute concurrently.

lookup_partition.description:
Separate per-item successes from failures in the lookup output. When true, the
action returns `{ "succeeded": [...item data...], "failed": [{ item, http_code?, error?, data? }] }`
instead of a flat array, so a poller can advance its cursor / mark items `seen`
only for successes and let failed items be retried on the next run. Failed items
are those whose iteration returned an HTTP code >= 400 or timed out.

## Example
```yaml
lookup_partition: true
```

state.description:
Persistent state operation (durable key/value): polling cursors, dedupe sets,
idempotency keys, counters. Backed by a pluggable backend (in-memory for local
single-node, Postgres for durable/shared, the AirPipe backend in managed mode).
Read state inline with `a|state::KEY|`.

## Example
```yaml
state:
  advance:
    key: last_seen
    value: a|Fetch::max_updated_at|
```

sftp.description:
Move files over SFTP: list a directory, fetch a file, write one, move or delete it.

## Example
```yaml
sftp:
  host: files.example.com
  user: airpipe
  private_key: a|secret::SFTP_KEY|
  host_key: "SHA256:kW8xDm2YuGv9NsLzalFWnMJ3j28XTnQJzw7/5GkE9+w"
  operation: list
  path: /incoming
```

only_new.description:
Keep only the records this config has not already handled.

Polling is the shape behind most "trigger" integrations — fetch a page on a
schedule, act on what is new, remember what you acted on. Every piece was already
here (`schedule`, `http`, `state.seen`), but assembling them meant iterating the
page with `lookup`, asking about each record separately and gating on the answer:
correct, verbose, and one state round trip per record.

## Example
```yaml
- name: NewOrders
  input: a|Fetch->orders|
  only_new:
    id: .id
    key: orders
    ttl: 30d
```

discover.description:
Discover the live members of a service — container endpoints, pods,
replicas — as an array, so a later action can fan out over them with
`lookup:` instead of a hard-coded address list.

## Example
```yaml
- name: Members
  discover:
    kubernetes:
      label_selector: app=api
      port_name: http
- name: PollAll
  lookup: a|Members|
  actions:
    - name: Health
      http:
        url: a|body::url|/healthz
```

delay.description:
Pause before continuing. Accepts a duration string (`"2s"`, `"500ms"`, `"1m"`, `"1d"`)
or a number of milliseconds.

Short and long delays behave differently, and the difference matters. Up to
`AIRPIPE__MAX_DELAY_SECS` (default 300s) the run simply sleeps — pacing between steps.
Past that a sleep would be the wrong instrument, so the run is **suspended** instead:
what has completed is written to a durable store, the caller is answered `202` with a
run id, and the scheduler resumes the rest when it comes due. Nothing is held open and
a restart does not lose the run.

Suspending needs somewhere to write. Managed has one; self-hosted needs
`AIRPIPE__DATABASE_URL`. Without it a long delay is **refused** rather than quietly
shortened into a sleep a restart would drop.

A delay wakes once, at the time you asked for. If you are waiting on work that might
not be finished by then, poll for it instead — an `assert` that fails until the job
reports done, plus a `retry`, which suspends between attempts in the same way.

## Example
```yaml
# sleeps in process
delay: "2s"

# suspends the run and resumes it tomorrow
delay: "1d"
```

wait_for_callback.description:
Suspend the run until something outside calls back — an approval, a signature, a
third-party webhook saying the job is done.

Unlike `delay`, which waits for a time you chose, this waits for an event you cannot
predict. The run is parked in the durable store and the caller is answered `202`; when
`POST /_ap/resume/<token>` arrives the run continues from the next action, and whatever
was posted becomes this action's output.

The token is yours to choose, and must be unguessable — anyone holding it can resume
the run. Mint one with `a|uuid|` in an earlier action and build the link from it:

## Example
```yaml
- name: Ticket
  json_output: '{"token": "a|uuid|"}'

- name: AskApprover
  email:
    to: approvals@example.com
    subject: Approve this refund
    body: 'Approve: https://api.example.com/_ap/resume/a|Ticket::token|'

- name: Approval
  wait_for_callback:
    token: a|Ticket::token|
    timeout: "7d"

- name: Refund
  run_when_succeeded: [Approval]
  http:
    url: https://api.example.com/refunds
    body: '{"approved_by": "a|Approval::approver|"}'
```

ws_publish.description: Publish a payload to realtime WebSocket channels (server push / fan-out).

mqtt_publish.description: Publish a payload to MQTT topics (pipeline → topic, cross-node fan-out).

agent.description:
Run a tool-calling AI agent loop: ask a model, run whatever tools it asks for,
feed the results back, repeat until it answers or the iteration budget runs out.

The tools are **this config's own interfaces**. Their JSON Schemas come from the
asserts those interfaces already declare, so a tool is documented, validated and
callable over HTTP and MCP by the same definition — there is no second place to
describe it, and nothing to keep in step.

## Example
```yaml
- name: Assistant
  agent:
    url: https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions
    model: gpt-4o-mini
    headers:
      authorization: "Bearer a|ap_var::OPENAI_API_KEY|"
    system: "You help staff answer order questions."
    input: a|body::messages|
    tools: [orders/search, orders/refund]
    max_iterations: 6
```

code.description:
Run JavaScript over this action's input.

The script gets `items` (or `item` in `each_item` mode), the results of earlier actions
through `$('ActionName')`, and a standard JS environment — `Buffer`, timers, `Intl`,
`DateTime`, `URL`, the text encoders. It does not get `require`, modules, the filesystem
or a socket: reaching outward is the `http:` action, or an interface called as a tool,
so retries, timeouts and metering still apply.

Bounded by `timeout_ms` and `memory_bytes`, both capped by the organisation's
entitlement, so a config cannot raise its own ceiling.

## Example
```yaml
- name: Normalise
  code: |
    return items.map(i => ({ json: { id: i.json.id, total: i.json.amount * 1.1 } }));
```

multi.description:
Run this action's `query` as a multi-statement batch (Postgres only).

The native driver prepares every query, and a prepared statement can hold
only one command — so a `query` with several `;`-separated statements
(e.g. a schema/seed block) normally fails with SQLSTATE 42601. Set
`multi: true` to run it via the simple protocol instead, which executes
all statements. Only valid for queries with **no** `params` (a batch
cannot be parameterized); it returns an empty result set.

## Example
```yaml
multi: true
query: |
  CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS a (id int);
  CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS b (id int);
```

Test.description:
Test definition for asserting conditions against a resolved value.
Tests support value resolution (via `value`, `jq`, `pointer`, or `action`),
type-aware comparisons, pattern matching, and structural schema validation.

When used inside an `assert` block, multiple tests run concurrently.
When used inside `verify_schema` via `FieldType.validate`, the test
runs against the leaf value at that schema path.

## Example - Basic value checks
```yaml
tests:
  - value: email
    is_not_empty: true
    regex: "^[^@]+@[^@]+\\.[^@]+$"
    error_message: "Invalid email"
    http_code_on_error: 422
```

## Example - Numeric comparisons
```yaml
tests:
  - value: age
    data_type: Number
    is_greater_than: 0
    is_less_than: 150
  - value: count()
    is_greater_than_or_equal_to: 1
```

## Example - Using jq for nested access
```yaml
tests:
  - jq: ".data.users | length"
    data_type: Number
    is_greater_than: 0
```

## Example - Cross-action reference
```yaml
tests:
  - action: FetchUser
    value: email
    is_not_null: true
```

## Example - Allowed/disallowed values
```yaml
tests:
  - value: status
    contains:
      allowed:
        - "active"
        - "pending"
        - "suspended"
      disallowed:
        - "deleted"
```

## Example - Schema validation with deep nested assertions
```yaml
tests:
  - verify_schema:
      disallow_unknown_keys: true
      structure:
        email:
          data_type: String
          validate:
            is_not_empty: true
            regex: "^[^@]+@[^@]+\\.[^@]+$"
        age:
          data_type: Number
          validate:
            is_greater_than: 0
        settings:
          theme:
            data_type: String
          notifications:
            data_type: Boolean
```

name.description: Human-readable name for identifying this test in logs and error output.

description.description: Description of what this test validates.

value.description:
JSON path to the target value within the input data (e.g., `email`, `user.name`).
Also supports `count()`: elements of an array, keys of an object, characters of a
string, 0 for null. It works the same way with `action:`, against that action's data.

## Example
```yaml
value: email             # simple key
value: user.address.city # nested path
value: count()           # how many
```

action.description:
Reference a previous action's output as the target value.

## Example
```yaml
action: FetchUser
value: email          # key within that action's output
```

action_value.description:
Reference a previous action's output using interpolation syntax. The full marker
grammar applies — paths, `jq::`, and filters — and the result keeps its JSON type.

## Example
```yaml
action_value: a|FetchUser::email|
action_value: a|Rows->length|
```

custom_value.description:
Override the target value with a custom literal string.

## Example
```yaml
custom_value: "some_static_value"
is_equal_to: "some_static_value"
```

jq.description:
Extract the target value using a jq filter expression.

## Example
```yaml
jq: ".users[0].email"
is_not_empty: true
```

pointer.description:
Extract the target value using a JSON pointer (RFC 6901).

## Example
```yaml
pointer: "/data/0/email"
is_not_empty: true
```

http_code_on_error.description:
HTTP status code to return when this specific test fails.
Takes precedence over the parent `Assert.http_code_on_error`.

success_message.description: Message returned when this test succeeds.

error_message.description:
Custom error message when this test fails. Replaces the default
auto-generated error detail.

## Example
```yaml
value: email
is_not_empty: true
error_message: "Email address is required"
```

hide_errors.description: Suppress error details from the response output for this test.

http_response.description: Static HTTP response value to return when this test is evaluated.

case_insensitive.description:
Enable case-insensitive matching for `is_equal_to` and `contains` checks.

## Example
```yaml
value: status
is_equal_to: "active"
case_insensitive: true    # matches "Active", "ACTIVE", etc.
```

is_equal_to.description:
Assert the value equals the expected value. Behavior varies by type:
strings compare as text, numbers as numeric value, booleans as bool,
arrays and objects compare as full JSON equality.

## Example
```yaml
is_equal_to: "active"      # string
is_equal_to: 42            # number
is_equal_to: true          # boolean
```
**Not for null.** `is_equal_to: null` asserts nothing — YAML null and an absent
key deserialise identically, so the check is skipped silently. Use `is_null: true`.

is_not_equal_to.description:
Assert the value does not equal the expected value.

## Example
```yaml
is_not_equal_to: "deleted"
```
**Not for null.** `is_not_equal_to: null` asserts nothing — see `is_equal_to`.
Use `is_not_null: true`.

is_less_than.description:
Assert the value is less than the threshold. For arrays, compares the length;
for numbers, the numeric value. A **string** needs `data_type` to say which is
meant — `Number` for its value, `String` for its length — and is an error
without one, because `"3650"` could be either.

## Example
```yaml
# String: fewer than 256 characters. The declaration is required --
# without it the engine cannot tell this from a value comparison.
value: title
data_type: String
is_less_than: 256

# Number: value under 100. Declare it too wherever the value can arrive
# as text -- a query parameter always does.
value: percentage
data_type: Number
is_less_than: 100

# Array: fewer than 10 elements. Arrays infer, so nothing to declare.
value: items
is_less_than: 10
```

is_less_than_or_equal_to.description:
Assert the value is less than or equal to the threshold.
Same type-dependent behaviour as `is_less_than`, including needing
`data_type` for a string.

is_greater_than.description:
Assert the value is greater than the threshold.
Same type-dependent behaviour as `is_less_than`, including needing
`data_type` for a string.

## Example
```yaml
# `age` can arrive as text from a query parameter, so say which reading
# is meant. Undeclared, a string here is an error.
value: age
data_type: Number
is_greater_than: 0
```

is_greater_than_or_equal_to.description:
Assert the value is greater than or equal to the threshold.
Same type-dependent behaviour as `is_less_than`, including needing
`data_type` for a string.

starts_with.description:
Assert the string value starts with the given prefix.

## Example
```yaml
value: url
starts_with: "https://"
```

ends_with.description:
Assert the string value ends with the given suffix.

## Example
```yaml
value: filename
ends_with: ".pdf"
```

contains_text.description: Assert the string contains at least one alphabetic character.

contains_number.description: Assert the string contains at least one numeric digit.

contains_upper.description: Assert the string contains at least one uppercase letter.

contains_lower.description: Assert the string contains at least one lowercase letter.

contains_special.description: Assert the string contains at least one special character.

contains.description:
Assert containment. Behavior varies by target type:
- **String**: substring match (or exact match in advanced/any mode)
- **Number**: substring match against the string representation
- **Array**: element membership
- **Object**: key existence

Supports three modes: standard (single value or array), advanced
(with `at_least` threshold), and any (with `allowed`/`disallowed` lists).

## Example - String substring
```yaml
value: email
contains: "@"
```

## Example - Array membership
```yaml
value: tags
contains: "featured"
```

## Example - Allowed values
```yaml
value: status
contains:
  allowed:
    - "active"
    - "pending"
  disallowed:
    - "deleted"
```

## Example - At least N matches
```yaml
value: roles
contains:
  values:
    - "admin"
    - "editor"
    - "viewer"
  at_least: 1
```

like.description:
SQL LIKE-style pattern matching (case-sensitive). Uses `%` as wildcard.

## Example
```yaml
value: name
like: "John%"         # starts with "John"
```

ilike.description:
SQL ILIKE-style pattern matching (case-insensitive). Uses `%` as wildcard.

## Example
```yaml
value: email
ilike: "%@gmail.com"  # any Gmail address
```

not_contains.description:
Inverse of `contains` for the standard and advanced modes: assert the value does NOT
contain the specified content.

The `allowed`/`disallowed` mode is NOT inverted. Those list names carry their own
polarity, so they mean the same thing here as under `contains` — every value must be
in `allowed`, none may be in `disallowed`. Writing it under `not_contains` is
redundant rather than opposite; prefer `contains`.

## Example
```yaml
value: content
not_contains: "<script>"
```

regex.description:
Assert the string value matches a regular expression pattern.

## Example
```yaml
value: phone
regex: "^\\+?[1-9]\\d{1,14}$"
```

is_not_null.description:
Assert the value is not null.

## Example
```yaml
value: user_id
is_not_null: true
```

is_not_empty.description:
Assert the value is not empty. Checks strings, arrays, and objects.

## Example
```yaml
value: name
is_not_empty: true
```

is_null.description:
Assert the value is null (when `true`) or is not null (when `false`).

## Example
```yaml
value: deleted_at
is_null: true         # must be null

value: email
is_null: false         # must not be null
```

is_uuid.description:
Assert the value is a valid UUID string.

## Example
```yaml
value: id
is_uuid: true
```

is_array.description:
Assert the value is a JSON array.

## Example
```yaml
value: items
is_array: true
```

is_empty.description:
Assert the value is empty: an empty string, an empty array, an empty object, or
null. The inverse of `is_not_empty`, which existed without it.

## Example
```yaml
value: middle_name
is_empty: true
```

is_string.description:
Assert the value is a string.

## Example
```yaml
value: user_id
is_string: true
```

is_number.description:
Assert the value is a number. A numeric *string* does not satisfy this — use
`regex` if you mean "looks like a number".

## Example
```yaml
value: quantity
is_number: true
```

is_boolean.description:
Assert the value is a boolean.

## Example
```yaml
value: enabled
is_boolean: true
```

is_object.description:
Assert the value is an object.

## Example
```yaml
value: address
is_object: true
```

is_in.description:
Assert the value is one of a fixed set.

This is the opposite direction from `contains`: `contains` asks whether the
target holds a given item, `is_in` asks whether the target is a member of a list
you supply. Comparison is deep, so objects and arrays can be members.

## Example
```yaml
value: status
is_in: [200, 201, 204]
```

not_in.description:
Assert the value is not one of a fixed set.

## Example
```yaml
value: role
not_in: ["banned", "deleted"]
```

is_between.description:
Assert a number — or the size of an array or object — falls within an
inclusive range.

## Example
```yaml
value: age
data_type: Number
is_between: { min: 18, max: 120 }
```

data_type.description:
One of `Number`, `String`, `Array` or `Object`, case-insensitive — what this value
is, so a comparison does not have to guess. Required when ordering a string.

Not the same thing as the `DataType` on an http or command action, which selects a
payload format (`text`, `json`, `csv`, `xml`).

The ordering operators — `is_greater_than` and friends — need to know whether
they are being asked about a value or a size, and the runtime type cannot tell
them: query parameters, form fields, headers and CSV columns all deliver numbers
as strings, so "it arrived as a string" does not mean "compare its length".

Declaring the type settles it:

```yaml
- value: older_than_days     # arrives as "3650" from the query string
  data_type: Number          # so compare 3650, not the 4 characters
  is_less_than: 365

- value: password
  data_type: String          # so compare how many characters it has
  is_greater_than: 7
```

Accepts `Number`, `String`, `Array`, `Object` — the same names `verify_schema`
uses. `String` means the comparison is about **length**; `Array` and `Object`
mean **how many elements or keys**; `Number` means the value itself.

**Required when the value is a string.** Ordering a string without this is an
error, because the runtime type cannot say whether `"3650"` means the value 3650
or a length of 4 — query parameters, form fields, headers, CSV columns and
`NUMERIC`/`DECIMAL` database columns all deliver numbers as text.

Numbers, arrays and objects still infer from their runtime type and need no
declaration. Inside `verify_schema`, an ordering check in a `validate` block
inherits the field's own `type:` and needs nothing extra.

is_before.description:
Assert the value is strictly before the given moment.

## Example
```yaml
value: expires_at
is_before: now
```

is_after.description:
Assert the value is strictly after the given moment.

## Example
```yaml
value: created_at
is_after: now-24h
```

is_on_or_before.description:
Assert the value is before, or the same instant as the given moment.

## Example
```yaml
value: starts_at
is_on_or_before: "2026-12-31"
```

is_on_or_after.description:
Assert the value is after, or the same instant as the given moment.

## Example
```yaml
value: valid_from
is_on_or_after: "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"
```

is_same_time_as.description:
Assert the value is the same instant as the given moment.

## Example
```yaml
value: updated_at
is_same_time_as: a|Fetch->updated_at|
```

is_not_same_time_as.description:
Assert the value is a different instant from the given moment.

## Example
```yaml
value: modified_at
is_not_same_time_as: a|Original->modified_at|
```

is_date.description:
Assert the value parses as a date at all, in any of the accepted formats.

## Example
```yaml
value: published_at
is_date: true
```

not_regex.description:
Assert the string value does NOT match a regular expression. The negated form of
`regex`, which had `not_contains`, `not_starts_with` and `not_ends_with` as
counterparts but no negation of its own.

## Example
```yaml
value: comment
not_regex: "(?i)<script"
```

not_like.description:
SQL LIKE-style pattern that must NOT match (case-sensitive). Uses `%` as wildcard.

## Example
```yaml
value: email
not_like: "%@example.com"
```

not_ilike.description:
SQL ILIKE-style pattern that must NOT match (case-insensitive).

## Example
```yaml
value: email
not_ilike: "%@EXAMPLE.com"
```

is_email.description:
Assert the value parses as an email address.

## Example
```yaml
value: email
is_email: true
```

is_url.description:
Assert the value parses as an absolute URL with a scheme and a host.

## Example
```yaml
value: callback_url
is_url: true
```

is_ip.description:
Assert the value parses as an IPv4 or IPv6 address.

## Example
```yaml
value: client_ip
is_ip: true
```

is_valid_jwt.description:
Validate the value as a JWT token using the provided secret.
On success, decoded claims are stored in `ok_data` under the
key specified by `result_key` (default: `jwt_claims`).

## Example
```yaml
value: token
is_valid_jwt: "my_jwt_secret"       # HS256 secret (bare string), or an object:
# is_valid_jwt: { jwks_url: "...", alg: RS256, iss: "...", aud: "..." }
result_key: user_claims
```

is_valid_hmac.description:
Verify an HMAC signature. The `value` field should point to the signature
received in the request (e.g. `x-hub-signature-256`). The assertion
recomputes HMAC over `body` using `secret` and compares against the target.

## Example (GitHub webhook)
```yaml
value: x-hub-signature-256
is_valid_hmac:
  secret: a|env::GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET|
  body: a|raw_body|
  algorithm: sha256   # sha1 | sha256 | sha512  (default: sha256)
  prefix: "sha256="   # stripped from target before comparison
```

is_valid_totp.description:
Assert the value is a currently-valid RFC 6238 time-based one-time password for the
shared secret — the second factor an authenticator app shows.

Fails closed: a target that is not a string (an absent header, a null field) is a
failure, never a pass.

## Example
```yaml
- value: body.code
  is_valid_totp:
    secret: a|secret::totp::user_seed|
    skew: 1        # also accept the code from one step either side
```

is_authorization.description:
Parse an HTTP Authorization header value. Supports `Basic` (decodes
base64 username:password) and `Bearer` (extracts token). Decoded
data is stored in `ok_data` keyed by scheme name.

## Example
```yaml
value: authorization
is_authorization: true
```

result_key.description:
Key name for storing extracted data (e.g., JWT claims) in the
action's ok_data output.

expression.description:
Evaluate a string expression as a boolean condition.
Supports interpolation via `a|...|` syntax before evaluation.

## Example
```yaml
expression: "a|body::count| > 0"
```

compare_value.description:
Compare the target value against another value or file for structural
differences. Supports JSON, XML, and string comparison with optional
field exclusions.

## Example - Compare against inline target
```yaml
compare_value:
  target: '{"status": "ok"}'
  data_type: json
  ignore_fields:
    - timestamp
```

## Example - Compare against file
```yaml
compare_value:
  file_path: "/path/to/expected.json"
  data_type: json
```

bcrypt_verify.description: Verify a plaintext value against a bcrypt hash. Deprecated: use `verify_bcrypt`.

verify_bcrypt.description:
Verify a plaintext value against a bcrypt hash.

## Example
```yaml
value: password
verify_bcrypt: "$2b$12$LJ3m..."
```

verify_signature.description:
Verify an Ed25519 signature against the target value.

## Example
```yaml
value: request_body
verify_signature:
  public_key: "a1b2c3..."    # hex-encoded Ed25519 public key
  signature: "d4e5f6..."     # hex-encoded signature
```

verify_schema.description:
Validate the value against a structural schema with recursive type
checking and optional per-field assertions. Supports nested objects,
arrays, and leaf-level validation via the `validate` field on each
`FieldType`.

## Example - Flat structure
```yaml
verify_schema:
  disallow_unknown_keys: true
  structure:
    name:
      data_type: String
      validate:
        is_not_empty: true
    age:
      data_type: Number
      validate:
        is_greater_than: 0
    active:
      data_type: Boolean
```

## Example - Nested objects with validation
```yaml
verify_schema:
  structure:
    user:
      email:
        data_type: String
        validate:
          is_not_empty: true
          regex: "^[^@]+@[^@]+\\.[^@]+$"
      settings:
        theme:
          data_type: String
          validate:
            contains:
              allowed:
                - "light"
                - "dark"
                - "system"
        notifications:
          data_type: Boolean
```

## Example - Array with positional validation
```yaml
verify_schema:
  structure:
    - id:
        data_type: Number
        validate:
          is_greater_than: 0
      title:
        data_type: String
        validate:
          is_not_empty: true
          is_less_than: 256
```

semver_matches.description:
Assert the string value satisfies a semver version constraint.

## Example
```yaml
value: api_version
semver_matches: ">=1.0.0, <2.0.0"
```

size_limit.description:
Assert the serialized byte size of the value does not exceed a limit.
Accepts human-readable sizes (e.g., `1 MB`, `500 KB`) or raw byte counts.

## Example
```yaml
value: payload
size_limit: "1 MB"
```

ContainOptions.description:
Containment check options. Supports three modes depending on the YAML structure
provided: standard (single value or array), advanced (with `at_least` threshold),
and any (with `allowed`/`disallowed` lists).

## Example - Standard single value
```yaml
contains: "search_term"
```

## Example - Standard array (match at least one)
```yaml
contains:
  - "admin"
  - "editor"
```

## Example - Advanced (at least N matches)
```yaml
contains:
  values:
    - "read"
    - "write"
    - "delete"
  at_least: 2
```

## Example - Allowed/disallowed lists
```yaml
contains:
  allowed:
    - "active"
    - "pending"
  disallowed:
    - "banned"
```

anyOf.description:
Allowed/disallowed list mode. Target must match an allowed value
and must not match any disallowed value.
Advanced mode with explicit value list and minimum match threshold.
Standard mode: a single value or array of values to check for containment.

ContainsAny.description:
Allowed/disallowed containment check. For strings, checks exact match against
each list. For arrays, checks that all elements are in `allowed` and no
elements are in `disallowed`.

## Example
```yaml
contains:
  allowed:
    - "published"
    - "draft"
    - "archived"
  disallowed:
    - "deleted"
    - "banned"
```

allowed.description: Values the target is allowed to match.

disallowed.description: Values the target must not match.

ContainsAdv.description:
Advanced containment check with a minimum match threshold.

## Example
```yaml
contains:
  values:
    - "read"
    - "write"
    - "admin"
  at_least: 2             # target must match at least 2 of the listed values
```

values.description: List of candidate values to check against.

at_least.description: Minimum number of values that must match for the check to pass.

JwtConfig.description:
Configuration for the `is_valid_jwt` assertion.

Accepts either a bare string (the HS256 shared secret — the original form,
still supported) or an object for asymmetric algorithms and OIDC providers:

```yaml
# HS256 (unchanged):
is_valid_jwt: "my-shared-secret"

# RS256/ES256 with a static PEM public key:
is_valid_jwt:
  alg: RS256
  public_key: a|ap_var::IDP_PUBLIC_KEY|

# RS256/ES256 verified against a provider's rotating JWKS (Auth0/Clerk/Cognito):
is_valid_jwt:
  jwks_url: https://YOUR.auth0.com/.well-known/jwks.json
  alg: RS256          # optional; falls back to the token header's alg
  iss: https://YOUR.auth0.com/
  aud: https://your-api
```

anyOf.description: Structured verification config for HS*/RS*/ES*/EdDSA and JWKS.

JwtVerifyConfig.description:
Structured form of [`JwtConfig`] — a symmetric secret, a static public key,
or a JWKS URL, plus optional algorithm and issuer/audience checks.

secret.description: HS256/384/512 shared secret. Mutually exclusive with `public_key`/`jwks_url`.

public_key.description: PEM-encoded public key for RS*/ES*/EdDSA verification (no network calls).

jwks_url.description:
URL of a JWKS document; the signing key is selected by the token's `kid`.
Fetched once and cached (with a short TTL), so provider key rotation is handled.

alg.description:
Signature algorithm, e.g. `HS256`, `RS256`, `ES256`, `EdDSA`. Required for
`public_key`; for `jwks_url` it defaults to the token header's `alg`.

iss.description: Expected `iss` claim. When set, tokens with a different issuer are rejected.

aud.description: Expected `aud` claim. When set, tokens with a different audience are rejected.

body.description:
The message to authenticate. Use `a|raw_body|` for webhook signature
verification so the bytes match exactly what the sender signed.

prefix.description:
Optional prefix to strip from the target value before comparing.
GitHub uses `"sha256="`, Stripe uses `"v1="`.

encoding.description:
How the signature in the target value is encoded: `hex` (default) or
`base64`. GitHub, Stripe and Slack send hex; Shopify sends standard
base64 in `X-Shopify-Hmac-Sha256`.

secret.description: The shared secret, base32 by default — the form an authenticator app hands out.

skew.description:
How many steps either side of now to also accept. Default 1, which absorbs the
clock drift and human latency that make a strictly-current-step check reject codes
that were correct when they were typed. Each extra step widens the window a stolen
code stays usable in, so keep it small.

CompareValue.description:
Value comparison configuration for diffing against an expected value.
Supports inline target strings or file paths, with optional field exclusions.

## Example - Inline comparison
```yaml
compare_value:
  target: '{"status": "ok", "code": 200}'
  data_type: json
  ignore_fields:
    - timestamp
    - request_id
```

## Example - File comparison
```yaml
compare_value:
  file_path: "./fixtures/expected_response.json"
  data_type: json
```

target.description: Inline string value to compare against.

data_type.description: Data format for comparison parsing: `json`, `xml`, or `string`.

ignore_fields.description: Fields to exclude from the comparison.

file_path.description: Path to a file containing the expected value.

data_type.description: Data format for comparison parsing: `json`, `xml`, or `string`.

ignore_fields.description: Fields to exclude from the comparison.

VerifySignature.description:
Ed25519 signature verification parameters.

## Example
```yaml
value: request_body
verify_signature:
  public_key: "a1b2c3d4e5f6..."     # hex-encoded Ed25519 public key
  signature: "f6e5d4c3b2a1..."       # hex-encoded signature bytes
```

signature.description: Hex-encoded signature bytes to verify against the target value.

VerifySchema.description:
Schema validation configuration. Validates a JSON value against a recursive
type structure with optional per-field assertions and unknown key rejection.

## Example - Basic object validation
```yaml
verify_schema:
  disallow_unknown_keys: true
  structure:
    name:
      data_type: String
      validate:
        is_not_empty: true
    email:
      data_type: String
      validate:
        regex: "^[^@]+@[^@]+\\.[^@]+$"
    age:
      data_type: Number
      validate:
        is_greater_than: 0
        is_less_than: 150
```

## Example - Nested with unknown key rejection
```yaml
verify_schema:
  disallow_unknown_keys: true
  structure:
    user:
      name:
        data_type: String
      role:
        data_type: String
        validate:
          contains:
            allowed:
              - "admin"
              - "editor"
              - "viewer"
    metadata:
      created_at:
        data_type: Number
      version:
        data_type: String
        validate:
          semver_matches: ">=1.0.0"
```

## Example - Array of objects (positional)
```yaml
verify_schema:
  structure:
    - id:
        data_type: Number
        validate:
          is_greater_than: 0
      status:
        data_type: String
        validate:
          is_not_empty: true
      settings:
        category:
          data_type: String
        featured:
          data_type: Boolean
```

disallow_unknown_keys.description:
When `true`, any keys present in the value but not defined in the schema
are reported as errors. Applies recursively to all nested objects.

structure.description:
The expected structure definition. Can be a nested object map, a positional
array, or a single leaf field type.

ValueType.description:
Schema value type for recursive structural validation. Represents either
a leaf field with a type constraint, a nested object with named fields,
or a positional array of typed elements.

## Example - Leaf field
```yaml
email:
  data_type: String
  validate:
    is_not_empty: true
```

## Example - Nested object
```yaml
user:
  name:
    data_type: String
  settings:
    theme:
      data_type: String
```

## Example - Positional array
```yaml
structure:
  - name:
      data_type: String
    id:
      data_type: Number
```

anyOf.description: Leaf field with type constraint and optional validation.
Nested object where each key maps to another `ValueType`.
Positional array where each index maps to a `ValueType`.

FieldType.description:
Leaf field definition within a `verify_schema` structure. Specifies the
expected data type and optional validation assertions that run against
the resolved value at this path.

Supported types: `String`, `Number`, `Boolean`, `Array`, `Object`, `Null`, `Any`.

## Example - Type check only
```yaml
email:
  data_type: String
```

## Example - Type check with assertions
```yaml
rating:
  data_type: Number
  validate:
    is_greater_than_or_equal_to: 0
    is_less_than_or_equal_to: 5
```

## Example - String with pattern and length
```yaml
slug:
  data_type: String
  validate:
    is_not_empty: true
    regex: "^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$"
    is_less_than: 128
```

## Example - Enum-like string constraint
```yaml
status:
  data_type: String
  validate:
    contains:
      allowed:
        - "published"
        - "draft"
        - "archived"
```

data_type.description:
Expected data type. One of: `String`, `Number`, `Boolean`, `Array`,
`Object`, `Null`, `Any`.

Named `data_type` to match the assert-level field of the same name, because it
answers the same question and, since 2.0.0, feeds the same machinery: an ordering
check inside `validate` reads this rather than asking for a second declaration.
`type` is still accepted and always will be -- every config written before this
uses it.

validate.description:
Optional test assertions to run against the leaf value after the type
check passes. Uses the same `Test` definition as the normal assertion
system, giving full access to all checks (`is_equal_to`, `regex`,
`contains`, `is_greater_than`, etc.).

## Example
```yaml
validate:
  is_not_empty: true
  regex: "^[a-z0-9-]+$"
  is_less_than: 64
```

Retry.description:
Try an action again when it fails.

Retry is also how you **poll**. An upstream job that is still running answers `200` with a
status that is not "done" — a success as far as HTTP is concerned — so pair `retry` with an
`assert` that fails until the job reports finished, and the action repeats until the answer
changes rather than only after an error.

A poll is a series of short waits whose total is long, so once they add up past
`AIRPIPE__MAX_DELAY_SECS` the run is **suspended** between attempts instead of sleeping
through them: parked in the durable store, the request closed, resumed by the scheduler for
the next attempt. A job that finishes quickly never touches the store; one that does not is
polled for as long as `attempts × delay` allows without holding anything open. The budget
is spent across resumes, not restarted by them, so a job that never finishes still stops.

Suspending needs a durable store — managed has one, self-hosted needs
`AIRPIPE__DATABASE_URL`. Without one the waits simply happen in process as before.

## Example
```yaml
# poll a render every minute for up to 40 minutes, suspending between attempts
assert:
  tests:
    - value: body.status
      is_equal_to: completed
retry:
  attempts: 40
  delay: 60000
```

attempts.description:
How many times to attempt the action in total, including the first try.
`1` (the default) means no retry.

delay.description:
Milliseconds to wait between attempts. With `exponential_backoff` this is the
base the delay grows from rather than a fixed pause.

exponential_backoff.description:
Double the wait after each failed attempt instead of using `delay` unchanged.
Worth setting against an upstream that is rate limiting or overloaded, where
retrying at a fixed interval keeps the pressure on.

on.description:
Which failures are worth repeating. Accepts codes (`429`), classes (`5xx`),
`any`, and the transport classes `timeout` / `connect`.

Unset uses the default set — `408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504` plus transport
failures — which is the intersection of what Polly, the AWS and Azure SDKs and
urllib3 all treat as transient. A 400 or a 401 will never succeed on a second
attempt, so repeating it only wastes the upstream's capacity and your own.

except.description:
Subtracted from whatever `on` resolves to, including the default set. Use it to
carve an exception out without restating the whole list.

respect_retry_after.description:
Honour a `Retry-After` response header when the upstream sends one (RFC 9110
§10.2.3), in preference to the computed backoff. Defaults to true: a server that
tells you when to come back knows better than a fixed curve does.

jitter.description:
Randomisation applied to the computed backoff. Defaults to `full`, per AWS's
"Exponential Backoff and Jitter": without it, every client that failed together
retries together, and the recovering upstream is hit by the same synchronised
wave it just fell over to.

max_delay.description:
Upper bound on a single wait, in milliseconds. Without it, exponential backoff on
a late attempt can schedule a wait longer than any caller is willing to hold for.

Jitter.description: How much randomisation to apply to a retry delay.

oneOf.description: Sleep a random duration in `[0, computed]` — AWS's "full jitter", the default.
Sleep exactly the computed backoff. Predictable, and synchronises clients.

timeout.description: How long to let the command run before it is killed, e.g. `30s`, `2m`.

name.description: Label for this command in traces and logs. Cosmetic — it does not affect the run.

shell.description:
Shell to execute `run` with. Defaults to the platform shell; set it when the
command depends on a specific one.

run.description:
The command line to execute.

```yaml
run: curl -s https://example.com/health
```

parse.description:
How to read the command's stdout. Unparsed output stays a plain string, so set
this when the command emits structured data you want to use downstream.

parse_stderr.description: How to read stderr, when the command reports structured errors there.

expect_exit.description:
Which exit codes count as a SUCCESSFUL action. Defaults to `0`.

An exit code is a command's own failure signal, exactly as a status code is an HTTP
server's, so it decides the action's outcome the same way — which is what makes
`retry`, `run_when_failed` and error branches work against a failing command.
Accepts one code (`0`), a list (`[0, 2]`), or `any` for the old behaviour where the
exit code was ignored entirely.

oneOf.description:
Newline-delimited JSON — one complete JSON document per line.

Its own variant rather than a fallback when JSON parsing fails, because guessing would
mean a genuinely truncated document silently became "the lines that happened to parse".
The server says which it is, so we believe it.

ExitExpectation.description: `expect_exit:` — one code, a list of codes, or `any`.

anyOf.description:
Only `any` is meaningful here; anything else never matches, which is the safe way
for a typo to behave.

url.description:
The URL to call. Interpolation applies, so it can be built from earlier steps or
variables.

```yaml
url: https://api.example.com/users/a|params::id|
```

expect_status.description:
Which response statuses count as a SUCCESSFUL action. Defaults to `2xx`, so a
4xx/5xx fails the action — which is what makes `retry`, `run_when_failed` and
`http_code_inherit_error` work against a failing upstream.

Accepts a class (`2xx`), an exact code (`404`), a list (`[2xx, 404]`), or
`any` for the pre-1.x behaviour where the status was only ever data.
A failed action still carries its status, headers and body, so an error
branch can read them.

idempotency.description:
Send an idempotency key with this request, so a RETRY cannot be processed twice.

The engine sends the same key on every attempt of one action execution — that is
the whole point, and it is the part a config cannot do for itself: `a|uuid|` would
mint a fresh key per attempt, which is just a second charge.

digest_auth_pass.description:
Password for HTTP Digest authentication. Keep it in a secret or variable rather
than in the config: `a|ap_secret::UPSTREAM_PASS|`.

pass.description: Password for HTTP Basic authentication. As with digest, reference a secret.

proxy.description: Send this request through an HTTP proxy.

headers.description:
Request headers. Values interpolate, which is how a token is passed without
writing it into the config.

```yaml
headers:
  content-type: application/json
  authorization: Bearer a|ap_var::API_TOKEN|
```

body.description:
Request body. A mapping is sent as JSON; a string is sent as-is, which is what
you want for a pre-rendered payload.

base64_bytes.description: Send raw bytes decoded from base64, for binary uploads that are not multipart.

method.description:
HTTP method. Defaults to `GET`.

Deliberately a string rather than a closed set: the engine passes it through as
a token, so an extension method a private API expects still works. The common
ones are offered as examples.

data_type.description: How to encode the body and read the response. Inferred when unset.

bearer_auth.description:
Token for `Authorization: Bearer`. Reference a secret or variable rather than
writing the token into the config: `a|ap_var::API_TOKEN|`.

multipart.description:
A flat list of parts for a `multipart/form-data` request.

Each entry is one form part. Whether it is a text or binary part is determined
implicitly by which source field is provided:

- `value` → plain text part
- `b64` → binary part decoded from base64
- `file_path` → binary part read from disk (not allowed in managed/hosted mode)

`filename` and `mime` are always optional. When omitted on a binary part, `mime`
is guessed from the `filename` extension, falling back to `application/octet-stream`.

```yaml
multipart:
  - name: image
    b64: a|previous_action::body.image.data|
    filename: photo.png   # optional — sent as Content-Disposition filename
    mime: image/png       # optional — guessed from filename if absent
  - name: model
    value: gpt-image-1
  - name: prompt
    value: Transform into Studio Ghibli style
```

Idempotency.description:
Idempotency-key configuration for an HTTP action.

RFC 9110 §9.2.2 says a client should not automatically retry a non-idempotent request
"unless it has some means to know that the request semantics are actually idempotent...
or some means to detect that the original request was never applied". An idempotency
key is that means, and is being standardised as the `Idempotency-Key` header
(draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header). Providers differ on the header name —
Stripe uses `Idempotency-Key`, PayPal `PayPal-Request-Id` — so it is configurable.

key.description:
The key to send. Omit it and the engine generates a UUID per action execution,
reused across that execution's retries.

Set it to derive the key from your own data (`a|body::orderId|`) when the caller
may retry the whole workflow and you want those attempts deduplicated too — an
engine-generated key only covers retries WITHIN one execution.

header.description: Header to carry the key. Defaults to `Idempotency-Key`.

MultipartPart.description:
A single part in a `multipart/form-data` request.

Exactly one of `value`, `b64`, or `file_path` must be provided per part.
All other fields are optional.

name.description: Form field name — the `name` attribute sent in `Content-Disposition`.

value.description:
Plain text value. Use this for non-binary form fields.
Mutually exclusive with `b64` and `file_path`.

b64.description:
Base64-encoded binary data. Decoded before sending.
Mutually exclusive with `value` and `file_path`.

file_path.description:
Path to a file to read and send as binary data.
Not permitted in managed/hosted mode — use `b64` instead.
Mutually exclusive with `value` and `b64`.

filename.description:
Filename sent in the `Content-Disposition` header for this part (e.g. `photo.png`).
Optional for binary parts; not meaningful for plain text parts.

mime.description:
MIME type for this part (e.g. `image/png`, `application/pdf`).
If omitted on a binary part, guessed from `filename`'s extension.
Falls back to `application/octet-stream` when neither is available.

MultipartData.description: Deprecated: use [`MultipartPart`] via the `multipart` field instead.

MultipartFile.description: Deprecated: use [`MultipartPart`] via the `multipart` field instead.

MultipartText.description: Deprecated: use [`MultipartPart`] via the `multipart` field instead.

ProxyHeaders.description: Controls which headers are passed through from the incoming request.

anyOf.description: When true, pass through all incoming headers
When a list, pass through only the specified headers; empty list means pass none

StateAction.description:
A persistent state operation. State is durable key/value used for things like
polling cursors, dedupe sets, idempotency keys and counters — distinct from
`var::` variables, which are read-only config/secrets.

It is backed by a pluggable backend selected by deployment:
in-memory (local single-node, ephemeral), Postgres (durable/shared, BYO via
`global.databases`), or the AirPipe backend (managed). Redis is a planned backend.

Read state inline anywhere interpolation runs with `a|state::KEY|` or
`a|state::NAMESPACE.KEY|`. The default namespace is the config name.

## Example — read a cursor, fetch since it, advance it
```yaml
actions:
  - name: Cursor
    state:
      get:
        key: last_seen
        default: "1970-01-01T00:00:00Z"
  - name: Fetch
    http:
      url: "https://api.example.com/items?since=a|state::last_seen|"
  - name: SaveCursor
    state:
      advance:
        key: last_seen
        value: a|Fetch::max_updated_at|
```

oneOf.description:
Read a value by key. Output: `{ "value": <v>, "version": <n>, "found": <bool> }`.
Returns `default` (or null) when the key is absent or expired.

Upsert a value. Last-write-wins unless `expected_version` is set (optimistic
concurrency — the write fails with a conflict if the stored version differs).
Output: `{ "version": <n> }`.

Monotonically advance a cursor: stores `max(current, value)`. Numeric values are
compared numerically; otherwise lexically (works for ISO-8601 timestamps).
Never moves a cursor backwards, so it is safe without CAS. Output: `{ "version": <n>, "value": <v> }`.
Delete a key. Output: `{ "deleted": <bool> }`.

Check-and-add an id to a bounded dedupe set. Returns whether the id was new
(i.e. not seen before). Output: `{ "was_new": <bool> }`.

namespace.description: Optional namespace. Defaults to the config name.

default.description: Value to return when the key is absent or expired.

namespace.description: Optional namespace. Defaults to the config name.

ttl.description: Optional time-to-live, e.g. "1h", "30m", "7d". Omit for no expiry.

expected_version.description:
Optimistic concurrency: only write when the stored version matches this value.
Use `0` to require the key not to exist yet. Ignored by `advance`.

key.description: Key identifying the dedupe set (e.g. the trigger/source name).

id.description: The id to check and record (e.g. a record id or content hash).

namespace.description: Optional namespace. Defaults to the config name.

ttl.description: Optional time-to-live for the set, e.g. "7d".

Sftp.description: One SFTP operation against one server.

host.description: Hostname or address of the SFTP server.

password.description: Password. Use `a|secret::NAME|` rather than a literal.

private_key.description:
Private key in PEM/OpenSSH form, preferred over a password. Use
`a|secret::NAME|` rather than a literal.

private_key_passphrase.description: Passphrase for `private_key`, if it has one.

host_key.description:
The server's host key fingerprint, as `ssh-keygen -lf` prints it:
`SHA256:kW8xDm2YuGv9NsLzalFWnMJ3j28XTnQJzw7/5GkE9+w`.

**Required** unless `accept_any_host_key` is set. SSH's security rests on this
check: without it, anyone on the network path can answer the connection, take the
credentials sent to them, and proxy to the real server so that nothing looks wrong.

accept_any_host_key.description:
Connect without verifying the server's identity. Defaults to `false`.

Only for a server you reach over a network you already trust end to end. Setting it
means credentials in this action can be taken by a machine-in-the-middle.

timeout.description:
How long to wait to connect and how long the session may sit idle, e.g. `30s`.
Defaults to 30 seconds.

operation.description:
What to do: `list`, `get`, `put`, `delete`, `rename` or `mkdir`.

`list` returns an array of `{name, path, size, is_dir, modified}`, where
`modified` is epoch seconds — so it feeds `only_new` and the date operators
without a second convention.

path.description: The remote path the operation applies to.

encoding.description:
`text` (default) or `base64`. Use `base64` for anything that is not UTF-8 —
a `get` of a binary file as text is an error rather than mangled output.

OnlyNew.description:
Filter a list down to the records this config has not seen before.

Takes the action's `input` (a list, or a single record treated as a list of one),
works out each record's identity, and passes on only those whose identity is new —
recording them as it goes, in a single state write for the whole page.

id.description:
A jq expression selecting each record's identity. Defaults to `.id`.

Whatever it returns is compared as text, so a number, a string or a composite all
work. Use a composite when no single field is unique:

```yaml
id: '.user_id + "/" + .updated_at'
```

A record whose id comes back null or missing is passed through rather than
silently dropped — losing records because a field was misspelled is the failure
this is meant to prevent, not cause.

key.description: The dedupe set to remember ids in. Two actions sharing a key share their memory.

namespace.description: Optional namespace for the set. Defaults to the config name.

ttl.description:
How long an id stays remembered, e.g. `30d`. Without one it is remembered until
evicted by the size cap (the oldest 5000 ids are kept).

Set this to slightly longer than the window in which a source can re-present a
record. Too short and records are handled twice; too long only costs storage.

skip_when_empty.description:
Skip this action — and anything that depends on it — when nothing is new.
Defaults to `true`.

A poll that finds nothing new almost always wants to do nothing, and a skip is
how the engine already expresses that: dependents do not run, and it is reported
as a skip rather than a failure. Set `false` to have the action succeed with an
empty list instead, when the steps after it should run regardless.

Discover.description:
Discover the live members of a service — container endpoints, pods, replicas —
and hand them to the rest of the pipeline as an array.

The point is to stop hard-coding a list of addresses that changes every time
something scales, restarts or reschedules. A `discover` action returns one
entry per member, and any later action fans out across them with `lookup:`:

```yaml
actions:
  - name: Members
    discover:
      kubernetes:
        label_selector: app=api
        port_name: http

  - name: PollAll
    lookup: a|Members|
    lookup_partition: true          # -> { succeeded: [...], failed: [...] }
    actions:
      - name: Health
        http:
          url: a|body::url|/healthz
```

Every backend returns the SAME item shape, so a config written against one
orchestrator moves to another by changing only the backend block:

```json
{
  "name":      "api-7d9f8b6c5d-x2ktp",
  "address":   "10.42.1.3",
  "port":      8080,
  "url":       "http://10.42.1.3:8080",
  "source":    "kubernetes",
  "ready":     true,
  "namespace": "default",
  "node":      "worker-1",
  "image":     "example/api:1.4.0",
  "labels":    { "app": "api" }
}
```

Fields a backend cannot know are omitted rather than faked — DNS returns
addresses only, so it has no `labels`, `image` or `ready`. Filtering on a field
a backend does not provide therefore matches nothing, which is why
`label_selector` belongs to the backends that actually have labels.

dns.description:
Resolve a DNS name to every address behind it.

The portable option: no API access, no credentials, no RBAC, nothing to
mount. In Kubernetes point it at a **headless** Service (`clusterIP: None`)
and it returns one entry per ready pod; under Docker Compose point it at a
scaled service name and it returns one entry per container. Anything with
DNS works the same way.

Addresses only — no labels or image, so no label-based targeting.

kubernetes.description:
Query the Kubernetes API for pods.

The richest option: real label selectors, plus namespace, node, readiness
and image per pod. Requires a ServiceAccount with `list` on pods, bound
by a namespace-scoped Role — see
<https://docs.airpipe.io/docs/install/kubernetes>.

docker.description:
Query the Docker Engine API for containers.

For container hosts that are not Kubernetes: plain Docker, Compose, Swarm.
Requires access to the Docker socket, which is equivalent to root on that
host — mount it deliberately, read-only, and prefer DNS where it will do.

**Unix only.** The Engine is reached over a unix domain socket; on Windows
the daemon listens on a named pipe instead, so this backend returns an
error there. `dns` discovers the same Compose containers on every platform,
with no socket and no privilege.

static.description:
An explicit list of `host:port` entries.

Not discovery — the escape hatch for environments with none of the above,
and what tests pin against. Keeping it in the same shape means a config can
start static and move to real discovery without touching the actions that
consume it.

Accepts either a YAML sequence or a single comma-separated string, so the
whole list can come from ONE variable — which is how a member list is
usually configured, and how `AIRPIPE__WS_MESH_PEERS` already works:

```yaml
static: "10.0.0.1:8080, 10.0.0.2:8080"     # one variable
static: a|ap_var::MEMBERS|                 # ...including from a variable
static: ["10.0.0.1:8080", "10.0.0.2:8080"] # or a sequence
```

Empty and null entries are dropped rather than rejected. Configs are
re-parsed AFTER interpolation, so an entry whose variable resolves to
nothing (`a|ap_var::MEMBER_2->default()|`) arrives here as a bare `-`,
i.e. YAML null. Failing there would break the config only in the
environment where that variable happened to be unset — in production,
having passed every test.

include.description: Keep only members matching these patterns. Applied before `exclude`.

exclude.description:
Drop members matching these patterns.

Exclusion wins over inclusion, deliberately: when the two disagree the safe
reading of the operator's intent is "do not touch this one".

port.description:
Port to use when the backend does not supply one (DNS always, Kubernetes
when neither `port` nor `port_name` is set). Without it those members are
returned with no port and no `url`.

A number, or a marker that resolves to one — see [`DiscoverPort`].

scheme.description: Scheme used to build each member's `url`. Defaults to `http`.

cache_ttl_secs.description:
How long to reuse a result before querying again, in seconds. Defaults to
10; `0` disables caching.

This matters more than it looks. Without it, a discovery action on a
request-path interface issues an API call per request — a busy route turns
into a denial-of-service against your own API server. The cache is keyed by
the fully-resolved query, so different selectors do not share entries.

fail_when_empty.description:
Fail the action when discovery returns nothing. Defaults to false, so an
empty result is an empty loop rather than an error — a service legitimately
scaled to zero is not a failure. Set true when "no members" means something
is broken.

name.description:
The name to resolve — `airpipe-mesh`, `api.default.svc.cluster.local`, or a
Compose service name. A bare name takes the action's `port`; `name:port` is
honoured as written.

exclude_self.description:
Drop this node's own address from the results. Useful when a service
discovers its peers and should not call itself. Needs the address to
exclude, e.g. `a|env::POD_IP|`.

namespace.description:
Namespace to search. Defaults to the agent's own namespace, read from the
ServiceAccount token mount — so the common case needs no configuration and
stays inside the namespace-scoped RBAC that ships by default.

label_selector.description:
Standard Kubernetes label selector, e.g. `app=api,tier!=canary`. Passed
through to the API server, so the same syntax as `kubectl -l`.

port_name.description:
Take the port from a named container port (`http`, `metrics`). Preferred
over a hard-coded number: the name survives a port change.

ready_only.description:
Return only pods whose containers are all ready. Defaults to true — an
unready pod is one that has told you not to send it traffic.

labels.description:
Container labels to match, e.g. `com.docker.compose.service: api`. All
listed labels must match.

network.description:
Docker network whose address should be reported for each container. With
several networks attached and no choice made, the first is used.

socket.description:
Path or URL of the Docker Engine socket. Defaults to
`/var/run/docker.sock`.

DiscoverFilter.description:
Regex patterns matched against a member's fields. An unset field matches
everything; a field the backend does not populate never matches.

name.description: Regex against the member name (pod or container name).

image.description: Regex against the full image reference, including registry and tag.

DiscoverPort.description:
A port: a literal number, or a marker that resolves to one.

Every other field of a `discover` block interpolates, because they are
strings. A bare `u16` could not, so `port: a|ap_var::SERVICE_PORT|` did not
merely fail to resolve — the marker was still marker TEXT when serde reached
it, and the agent died at load with `invalid type: string ... expected u16`.
A config that names its port the same way it names everything else should
work, so the string form is accepted and parsed after interpolation.

anyOf.description:
`port: a|ap_var::SERVICE_PORT->default(8080)|`, or a quoted `"8080"`.
Still a marker at parse time; resolved once interpolation has run.

WaitForCallback.description:
Wait for something outside to call back before continuing.

Needs a durable run store, the same as a long `delay`: managed has one, self-hosted needs
`AIRPIPE__DATABASE_URL`. Without one the wait is refused rather than becoming an in-process
pause that a restart would lose.

token.description:
The secret that identifies this wait. Anyone holding it can resume the run, so it must
be unguessable — mint it with `a|uuid|` in an earlier action rather than using
something predictable like an order number.

timeout.description:
How long to wait before giving up, as a duration (`"7d"`, `"2h"`).

Required, and there is no unbounded option: a wait nobody ever answers would hold a row
forever. When it expires the action FAILS, so the actions after it do not run and the
timeout is visible rather than silently looking like an approval.

aws_ses.description:
Send through AWS SES using the engine's AWS credentials instead of SMTP.
Mutually exclusive with `smtp` in practice — set one or the other.

smtp.description: SMTP server to send through. Omit when using `aws_ses`.

from.description: Sender address. Must be one the SMTP server or SES identity is allowed to send as.

reply_to.description: Address replies should go to, when it differs from `from`.

rows.description:
Batch mode. An interpolation ref resolving to a JSON array of row objects
(e.g. `a|Fired|`). When set, one email is sent per row: each row's string
fields `to` / `subject` / `html` / `text` / `cc` / `bcc` supply that message
(build them in the producing query), while `from` and `smtp` are shared from
this action. `to`/`cc`/`bcc` may be comma-separated for multiple recipients.

header.description: Extra raw headers to attach to the message.

html.description:
HTML body. Send `html`, `text`, or both — both is the polite form, since a
client that cannot render HTML falls back to the text part.

params.description:
Positional values substituted into the body, for templates that use placeholders
rather than interpolation refs.

attachments.description:
Files to attach. Turns the message into a `multipart/mixed` — the html/text
body stays the first part and each attachment follows.

## Example
```yaml
attachments:
  - filename: signups.csv
    content: a|BuildCsv::csv_b64|   # base64 (see `b64_encode`)
    content_type: text/csv
```

EmailAttachment.description: One file attached to an outgoing email.

content.description:
The file contents. `base64` by default — pair it with the `b64_encode`
post-transform, which is also what makes binary files (PDF, images) work.
Use `encoding: utf8` to attach a plain string (CSV, JSON, text) directly.

name.description: Metric name (must be a valid Prometheus metric name).

value.description:
Value to record. Required for `gauge` and `histogram`; counters increment by 1 when omitted.
Accepts a literal number or a standard interpolation expression (`a|ActionName::field|`).
Numeric values resolved via interpolation retain their type — no string parsing required.

labels.description:
User-defined labels. `config`, `interface`, and `action` are always attached automatically.
Values accept standard interpolation expressions. Resolved values are coerced to strings
at emit time since Prometheus labels must be strings.

WsPublish.description:
Publish a payload to realtime WebSocket channels (server push / fan-out). Every
socket subscribed to any listed channel — on this node AND every peer node —
receives the payload. Fire-and-forget: it does not wait for delivery.

## Example
```yaml
- name: Broadcast
  ws_publish:
    channels: a|body::rooms|     # a string, an array, or an a|...| marker
    data: a|OrderAction|         # defaults to a|body| when omitted
```

channels.description:
Channel key(s) to publish to: a string, an array of strings, or an `a|...`
marker resolving to either.

data.description:
The payload pushed to subscribers. An `a|...` marker or inline JSON.
Defaults to the request/message body when omitted.

retain.description:
Store the payload as the channel's RETAINED value, so a subscriber that connects (or
reconnects) later immediately receives the current value on subscribe. Defaults to false.
Accepts a literal boolean OR an `a|...` marker resolving to one (e.g. `a|body::retain|`),
so a backend route can pass retain through per-request.

MqttPublish.description:
A `mqtt_publish` action publishes a message from a pipeline to one or more MQTT
topics. Every subscriber to a listed topic — on this node AND every peer node (via
the realtime mesh) — receives the payload. This is the pipeline→topic direction
(the inbound topic→pipeline direction is the ingest consumer). Fire-and-forget: it
does not wait for broker acknowledgement.

## Example
```yaml
- name: Push
  mqtt_publish:
    topics: a|body::topic|      # a string, an array, or an a|...| marker
    data: a|Reading|            # defaults to a|body| when omitted
    qos: 1                      # 0 (default) | 1 | 2
    retain: false               # default false
```

topics.description:
Topic(s) to publish to: a string, an array of strings, or an `a|...` marker
resolving to either.

data.description:
The payload published to subscribers. An `a|...` marker or inline JSON. A JSON
string publishes as raw text; any other value publishes as its JSON encoding.
Defaults to the request/message body when omitted.

qos.description:
MQTT quality of service for the published message: 0 (at most once, default),
1 (at least once), or 2 (exactly once).

retain.description:
Whether the broker retains this message as the topic's last-known-good value,
delivered to future subscribers on subscribe. Defaults to false. Accepts a literal
boolean OR an `a|...` marker resolving to one (e.g. `a|body::retain|`).

url.description:
An OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint. Anything speaking that shape works:
